experiments.question: Do the poor eat when water gets dear?
experiments.ruleChanged: Law 5 share 20 % (base) vs 0 % (changed). Both worlds have a drought: rain −70 % for 120 days from June of year 4. Prices are fully dynamic.
experiments.claim: With Law 5 at 20 %, nobody is short, everyone can still pay at least a day of basics each day, and dividends alone pay the owner-only cohort’s basics through the drought, which they do not at 0 %. (Law 5’s work here is the owner-only cohort’s income; the poorest tenth’s levels in both worlds are in the numbers.)
experiments.evidence: 20 %: short 0 person-days, lowest room 127.80 days of the bundle, owner-only dividends ≥ 1.81× the bundle. 0 %: short 0, room 310.96 days, dividends 0.00×. In the drought, water cost 3.06× its earlier price with Law 5 and 3.00× without. The lowest room to pay of anyone was 127.80 days of the basic bundle a day with Law 5 and 310.96 without. The poorest tenth by holdings lived at 11.13 R a day in the drought with Law 5 and 6.54 without; by Aven output, 6.79 and 6.63. Owner-only dividends paid 1.81× their basic bundle at worst with Law 5, and 0.00× without. Person-days short: 0 with Law 5, 0 without.
experiments.takeaway: In the drought, dividends paid the owner-only blobs’ basics 1.81× over with Law 5 and not at all without it, and nobody went short in either world.

experiments.ruleChanged: The owner-only cohort (5 %, Aven output 0, nothing held at the start) spends dividends and some of what it holds (base) vs dividends only (changed).
experiments.claim: Normal: never short from day 1. Strict: dividends alone pay the basic bundle by day 120, and the dividends-only cohort is never short after it.
experiments.evidence: normal short 0; dividends-only short 0 (after day 120: 0, last day -1); strict test from day 1. On dividends only, the owner-only blobs were never short of a basic. Spending some of what they hold as well, they were short 0 person-days. Dividends alone paid every member’s bundle every day from day 1. Their living standard in the last year: 1.35 on dividends only, 1.51 normally.

experiments.question: Where does the MIND end up?
experiments.ruleChanged: Treasuries pay their surplus above the 270-day reserve out for Aven work proposals (base) vs keep it (changed).
experiments.claim: Law 5 alone is not enough: with payout people hold most of the MIND, at least 20 points more than when treasuries keep their surplus.
experiments.evidence: people’s share 79.8 % (payout) vs 44.9 % (keep), gap 35.0 %. With payout, people held 79.8 % of all MIND at the end; when treasuries kept their surplus, 44.9 %. Treasuries held 13.0 % vs 49.3 %. The poorest decile lived at 13.88 with payout and 10.37 without.
experiments.takeaway: With payout, people ended up holding 80 % of all MIND; when treasuries kept their surplus, only 45 %.

experiments.question: Does inequality fade?
experiments.ruleChanged: Melt 7 % a year (base) vs 0 % (changed). In both worlds, holdings are made as unequal as Germany’s (Gini 0.72) at the start of year 9.
experiments.claim: The melt fades every advantage: with it, at least half the shock’s extra inequality is gone by the end, and the Gini ends lower than without the melt.
experiments.evidence: Gini 0.23 → 0.65 → 0.34 with melt; 0.23 → 0.65 → 0.41 without. The shock raised the Gini of holdings to 0.65. With the melt it fell to 0.34 by the end. Without the melt it fell to 0.41.
experiments.takeaway: After the shock the holdings Gini fell from 0.65 to 0.34 with the melt, and only to 0.41 without it.

experiments.question: What if a food COOP fails?
experiments.ruleChanged: Two food COOPs at genesis (base) vs one (changed). In both worlds the food COOP AGRI fails on day 300: its output drops to 10 % for a year.
experiments.claim: Two sellers of each basic keep everyone fed: with two food COOPs, nobody is short of food when one fails.
experiments.evidence: two food COOPs: 300 person-days short of food (the second seller was alive at the failure; receivership after 29 days); one: 3,100. With two food COOPs, people were short of food 300 person-days; with one, 3,100. The failing COOP went into receivership after 29 days (two sellers) and 29 days (one). The lowest food share anyone got was 83.3 % vs 70.2 %.
experiments.takeaway: When a food COOP failed, people were short of food on 300 person-days with two food COOPs and on 3,100 with one.

experiments.question: Can four friends cheat?
experiments.ruleChanged: Avens send HEARTS by delivered output per HEART (base) vs by the MIND’s pool price (changed). In both worlds, four friends open a COOP that makes nothing on day 365. They pay themselves 90 % of its treasury and buy its MIND to push its price.
experiments.claim: Avens that follow delivered output starve a ring: it gets less than under the price rule, and no more than its share of the people.
experiments.evidence: ring share of others’ HEARTS 0.2 % (output) vs 1.6 % (price); its share of people 4.0 %. Following delivered output, Avens sent the ring 0.2 % of others’ HEARTS; following the pool price, 1.6 %. The ring is 4.0 % of the people. Its members ended at 0.60× the others’ mean holding (output rule) and 0.39× (price rule).
experiments.takeaway: Avens that follow delivered output sent the ring 0.2 % of other people’s HEARTS; Avens that follow the pool price sent it 1.6 %.

experiments.question: Do newcomers eat?
experiments.ruleChanged: A constant population (base) vs +2 % a year (changed), on the same fixed land. Newcomers arrive with an Aven and nothing held.
experiments.claim: Growth raises rent, not hunger: newcomers are never short, and ground rent ends higher than with a constant population.
experiments.evidence: newcomers short 4548 of 14595 person-days; rent at the end 1.40e-2 (growth) vs 1.25e-2 (constant). With growth the village went from 100 to 117 people. Newcomers lived 14,595 person-days in their first three years and were short on 4,548. Ground rent went from 1.24e-4 to 1.40e-2 R a m² a day (constant population: 1.25e-2). The mean living standard ended at 25.56 vs 29.65.
experiments.takeaway: The village grew to 117 people; newcomers were short on 4,548 person-days, and ground rent ended 1.12× the rent with a constant population.
